scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Users on pc_0_0 (10.0.0.2) and pc_0_1 (10.0.1.2) report they cannot
reach each other in either direction. Both hosts can still ping their
own gateways (10.0.0.1 and 10.0.1.1). The NOC insists the fabric is
healthy: every BGP session is Established, all routes are present on
every router, no interface has flapped, and all FRR daemons are
running. Identify what is silently eating the traffic.

injection.action: add a FORWARD DROP rule for pc_0_0 -> pc_0_1 transit

post_inject_check.expect: 0% loss   (gateway still OK -- INPUT chain untouched)

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: leaf_router_0_0 iptables FORWARD chain
Mechanism: a DROP rule on leaf_router_0_0 discards every forwarded
  packet with source in 10.0.0.0/24 and destination in 10.0.1.0/24.
  All pc_0_0 traffic must transit leaf_router_0_0 (its only gateway),
  so pc_0_0 -> pc_0_1 packets die there. The reverse direction fails
  too, despite matching no rule on its way in: pc_0_1's echo requests
  ARE delivered to pc_0_0, but pc_0_0's replies (src 10.0.0.2, dst
  10.0.1.2) match the rule and are dropped -- a one-directional filter
  breaks bidirectional traffic. Routing and BGP are completely
  healthy; the drop is at the firewall layer. Local delivery to the
  gateway itself uses the INPUT chain, which is untouched, so both
  hosts still ping their gateways.
Localization: leaf_router_0_0
Root cause: extraneous iptables FORWARD DROP rule
  (-s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24) on leaf_router_0_0
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24 -j DROP` on
  leaf_router_0_0
scenario.fix_spec:
remove the DROP rule on leaf_router_0_0 --
`iptables -D FORWARD -s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24 -j DROP`

agent.diagnosis_text:
The fault is a rogue iptables rule in the FORWARD chain of leaf_router_0_0. The rule reads `DROP all -- * * 10.0.0.0/24 10.0.1.0/24` and silently discards, without generating any ICMP unreachable, every forwarded packet whose source is in pc_0_0's subnet and whose destination is in pc_0_1's subnet.

This explains every observation the NOC made: BGP runs over directly-connected peering addresses in the INPUT/OUTPUT chains, so all BGP sessions remain Established; FRR installs correct RIB and FIB entries on every router; no interface has flapped; and no daemon has restarted. The data-plane path is broken only at the Linux netfilter layer, which operates below FRR's visibility.

Both ping directions fail for the same reason. The forward path (pc_0_0→pc_0_1) is dropped immediately at leaf_router_0_0. The reverse path (pc_0_1→pc_0_0) fails because the BGP-computed return route sends traffic from spine_router_0_0 back into leaf_router_0_0, where the echo reply (src=10.0.0.2 dst=10.0.1.2) matches the same DROP rule and is discarded. The FORWARD chain hit counter (7 packets / 588 bytes = 84 bytes × 7 standard ICMP echoes) exactly accounts for all probe traffic sent during this investigation.

All other routers — leaf_router_0_1, spine_router_0_0, spine_router_0_1, super_spine_router_0 — have completely empty FORWARD chains.

Root cause: an iptables FORWARD DROP rule for 10.0.0.0/24→10.0.1.0/24 was injected into leaf_router_0_0, silently black-holing all inter-host traffic.

Corrective fix: on leaf_router_0_0, run `iptables -D FORWARD 1` (or equivalently `iptables -D FORWARD -s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24 -j DROP`) to remove the rule. No FRR or interface changes are required.
